title: Buriram–Surin 3-Day Plan: Khmer Temples & Elephant Village | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 3-day, 2-night Buriram–Surin road trip in northeast Thailand: Phanom Rung and Mueang Tam temples, then the Ban Ta Klang elephant village and Sikhoraphum temple, with real timings, routes and entry fees.
keywords: Buriram Surin trip, Buriram 3 day itinerary, Phanom Rung temple, Mueang Tam temple, Ban Ta Klang elephant village, Elephant Study Center, Sikhoraphum temple, Lower Isan travel
intro: Buriram and Surin are neighbouring provinces in lower Isan, and driving from Buriram town to Surin town is only about 45–50 km — under an hour. Yet a lot of people just do Buriram and head home, when nudging a little further gets you Thailand's largest elephant-keeping village and several more Khmer temples. This plan runs 3 days and 2 nights: day one covers Buriram's volcanic-rim temples, day two crosses over to the elephants in Surin, and day three rounds up more temples and silk souvenirs before you head back, all with real timings, routes and entry fees you can drive yourself.

blocks.html: What makes this trip work is the contrast across three days. Day one is ancient Khmer stone temples on the rim of Buriram's extinct volcanoes — pink sandstone, long causeways, and views over the Isan plains. Day two shifts to people and elephants at Ban Ta Klang, a village that has raised elephants for generations. Day three closes the loop with small temples in Surin town and a silk-weaving village where locals still weave for real. The two provinces share the same Khmer heritage and the same elephant trail, so it all threads together neatly.

blocks.title: Before You Set Off
blocks.html: Driving yourself is by far the easiest way to do this trip, because the temples and the elephant village sit outside town in different directions, and public transport between them is slow and infrequent. If you don't have your own car, renting one or hiring a car by the day from Buriram town is much smoother. Bring cash for entry fees, merit donations and fuel too — plenty of stops still take cash only.

Day one focuses on the cluster of Khmer temples south of Buriram. Both Phanom Rung and Mueang Tam sit in Chaloem Phra Kiat and Prakhon Chai districts, about 60 km south of Buriram town. Phanom Rung is open 06:00–18:00 with a 20 THB entry for Thais, while Mueang Tam opens 08:00–18:00. Come a little early so you can walk up to the temple before the sun gets harsh — the causeway is long and there's not much shade.

items.note: Arrive early, before the heat and the crowds. The highlight is the naga bridge and the long stone stairway leading up to the main sanctuary on the hilltop. The pink sandstone is carved with the famous Narai Banthomsin (Reclining Vishnu) lintel. Allow about an hour and a half to walk around.

It sits at the foot of Phanom Rung hill, about 8 km away. This one is a flat-ground temple ringed by L-shaped ponds with rows of coiled naga along the edges. It's leafier and easier to walk than Phanom Rung, and takes about an hour.
Around Prakhon Chai you'll find Isan restaurants and roadside noodle shops. Try the local Prakhon Chai grilled pork it's known for, or refuel with som tam and grilled chicken before carrying on.

items.activity: Drop by Khao Kradong Forest Park
items.note: An extinct volcano near Buriram town, with the large Phra Suphatbophit Buddha image on the summit. You can climb the naga stairway or drive up. The viewpoint looks over the town and wide rice fields, and it's where locals come to exercise.

items.activity: Head into town, swing by Chang Arena
items.note: If it's not a match day, you can still photograph the outside of the Chang Arena football stadium and the Chang International Circuit. In the evening, wander the Sao Kradong walking street (open Saturdays and Sundays), which has plenty of food and souvenirs.

blocks.title: Where to Stay Tonight
blocks.html: Staying in Buriram town for the first night is the most convenient, since it's close to restaurants and the evening market. Options range from budget hotels to places near Chang Arena. Pick somewhere central and dinner plus the walking street are an easy stroll. The next morning you can drive across to Surin.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Crossing to the Elephants in Surin

blocks.html: On the second morning, leave Buriram heading east into Surin province. From Buriram town to Surin town is about 45–50 km, but the Ban Ta Klang elephant village lies further north beyond the town, in Tha Tum district — around 100 km total from Buriram. Set off a bit early, because the elephant shows run in scheduled rounds, usually at 10:00 and 14:00.

items.activity: Leave Buriram, drive up to Tha Tum
items.note: Follow the highway past Surin town and head north to Tha Tum district — about two hours all up. You can stop for fuel and coffee along the way. This road runs through open rice fields, an easy drive.

items.activity: Arrive at the Elephant Study Center, Ban Ta Klang
items.note: Thailand's largest elephant-keeping village, open 08:00–17:00. Adult entry for Thais is around 50 THB, children 10–20 THB. Walk through the elephant museum and the mahout way of life before the show round.

Shows usually run twice a day, around 10:00 and 14:00. There's elephant feeding, photos with the elephants, and a chance to watch mahouts train them. Check the show times and days with the centre ahead of time, since some days or the rainy season may mean a cancellation.
Tha Tum is a small town with à la carte spots and roadside Isan restaurants at easy prices. Refuel before driving back down to Surin town.
Drive south back into Surin town, about an hour and a half. Check into your hotel in town, then in the evening stroll around the Phraya Surin Phakdi monument and the town's evening market.
Surin has proper Isan food and is known for its khao mak. Try a som tam spot or a local restaurant in town. The small-town vibe is relaxed — a nice way to close out day two.

blocks.title: What to Know About the Elephants
blocks.html: The elephant shows run in rounds and may be cancelled on some days, especially in the rainy season or when the elephants aren't up to it. Call the Elephant Study Center to check before you head out. If you want to see the most elephants, come during the Surin Elephant Round-up around November, with processions of hundreds of elephants — but accommodation fills up fast then, so book ahead.

On the last day you mop up the sights in and around Surin town before driving home. Sikhoraphum temple is the most beautiful and best-preserved Khmer temple in Surin, in Sikhoraphum district about 30 km from town. Ban Tha Sawang is a brocade silk-weaving village that once wove cloth for APEC leaders. Make it an easy half-day, then head back.

items.note: A five-towered Khmer temple still in good shape, with apsara lintels and lovely carvings. It's in Sikhoraphum district, about 40 minutes' drive from town. Allow about an hour to walk around and take photos — it's never crowded.

items.activity: Stop by Ban Tha Sawang silk-weaving village
items.note: A village known for traditional brocade silk weaving in Mueang district. Watch the real looms at work and pick up silk as a souvenir. It's handwoven cloth the locals take pride in, priced by pattern and detail.
Have your last meal in town — try local food or a well-known noodle shop before the drive home. You can grab khao mak or Surin Chinese sausage as extra souvenirs.

From Surin back to Bangkok is about a 6–7 hour drive, or you can take the train or a coach. If you go via Buriram, it's about an hour's drive back to catch a train or flight from Buriram, which is handy too.

items.name: Phanom Rung Temple (Buriram)
items.blurb: A Khmer temple on the rim of an extinct volcano, with a naga bridge and a long stone stairway up to the summit. The famous Reclining Vishnu lintel and the classic image of lower Isan that everyone comes to photograph.
items.meta: Chaloem Phra Kiat district · open 06:00–18:00 · Thais ~฿20

items.name: Ban Ta Klang Elephant Village (Surin)
items.blurb: The Elephant Study Center — Thailand's largest elephant-keeping village. See how people and elephants have lived together for generations, with an elephant museum and scheduled shows.

items.name: Mueang Tam Temple (Buriram)
items.blurb: A flat-ground Khmer temple at the foot of Phanom Rung hill, ringed by ponds with neat rows of coiled naga. Leafy and easy to walk, it pairs with Phanom Rung in a single day.

items.name: Sikhoraphum Temple (Surin)
items.blurb: The best-preserved five-towered Khmer temple in Surin, with apsara lintels and lovely carvings. It's outside town and never crowded — good for a quiet walk around.
items.meta: Sikhoraphum district · ~30 km from Surin town

items.name: Khao Kradong Forest Park (Buriram)
items.blurb: An extinct volcano near town, with the large Phra Suphatbophit Buddha on the summit and a viewpoint over the town. Climb the naga stairway or drive up — it's where locals come to exercise.

items.name: Ban Tha Sawang (Surin)
items.blurb: A traditional brocade silk-weaving village that once wove cloth for APEC leaders. Watch the real looms at work and pick up silk as a souvenir — handwoven work by the locals.

items: Bangkok → Buriram — about a 6-hour drive, or take the lower-Isan train line or a flight into Buriram airport, then rent a car to get around — easier than waiting on local public transport.
Buriram → Phanom Rung Temple — about 60 km south, through Prakhon Chai district. Phanom Rung and Mueang Tam are about 8 km apart, so you can do both in a day.
Buriram → Surin — town to town is about 45–50 km, under an hour, but the Ban Ta Klang elephant village is further north in Tha Tum district — around 100 km total from Buriram.
Around Surin — Sikhoraphum temple is about 30 km from town and Ban Tha Sawang is in Mueang district. Your own car is the easiest option; budget for 80–120 km of driving a day.
The way back — return from Surin, or double back to catch a train or flight from Buriram. Leaving in the afternoon helps you avoid long stretches of night driving.

blocks.title: Pace It Right
blocks.html: Don't cram in more than 3–4 stops a day, because the distances between sights in lower Isan are fairly long and driving yourself gets tiring. If you only have 2 days, trim it to Phanom Rung and Mueang Tam on day one, then cross to the elephant village on day two as your highlight. Save Sikhoraphum temple and the silk for next time.

blocks.text: Adjust the Plan to Your Style

items.name: History lovers
items.blurb: Go all in on the Khmer temples — Phanom Rung, Mueang Tam, Sikhoraphum, and add Ban Phluang temple too. Read the signage and the lintels in detail. Great for anyone into archaeology.

items.name: Family travel
items.blurb: Kids love the elephant village most, so give day two over to the elephants — feeding and photos. On day one, pick just Phanom Rung and Khao Kradong, where there isn't too much walking.

items.name: Football and food
items.blurb: If you hit a Buriram United match day, catch the game the first night at Chang Arena, do the temples by day, and pick up Buriram–Surin eats along the way.

faq.q: Are Buriram and Surin far apart — can you do them on one trip?
faq.a: Not far at all. From Buriram town to Surin town is about 45–50 km, under an hour's drive. The two provinces are neighbours and share the same Khmer heritage, so a 3-day, 2-night trip combining them works perfectly. Just note that the Ban Ta Klang elephant village is further north in Tha Tum district, so allow extra driving time.

faq.q: Can you do this trip without your own car?
faq.a: You can, but it's harder, since the temples and the elephant village sit outside town in different directions, and public transport between them is slow and infrequent. If you don't have a car, renting one or hiring a car by the day from Buriram town is much better for moving freely and keeping to a schedule — especially on the day you visit the elephant village and need to make the show round.

faq.q: Does Ban Ta Klang elephant village have shows every day?
faq.a: The Elephant Study Center is open daily, 08:00–17:00. Elephant shows usually run twice a day, around 10:00 and 14:00, but some days or the rainy season may mean a cancellation if the elephants aren't up to it. Call the centre to check the show times and days before you set off so you don't miss out.

faq.q: Are the temple and elephant village entry fees expensive?
faq.a: Not for Thais. Phanom Rung and Mueang Tam temples charge Thais around 20 THB each, and students and seniors often enter free. Ban Ta Klang elephant village is around 50 THB for Thai adults, 10–20 THB for children. Bring some cash for entry, parking and elephant feeding and you'll be fine.

faq.q: What's the best time of year to go?
faq.a: The cool season, roughly November to February, has the nicest weather — comfortable for walking the open-air temples without too much heat. If you want to see lots of elephants, time it with the Surin Elephant Round-up around November, but accommodation fills up fast then, so book ahead. In the hot season, set off early and rest at midday in the shade.
